title: A Bush in the Desert
lead: God can call a person who insists they are not fit for the job.
questions: Which excuse keeps coming back in your conversations with God, and what would today look like if you didn’t use it?
Which part of your life story do you consider wasted, and what would happen if God reached for exactly that part?
Whom do you think of as too far from God, even though He may be saying of them right now, “Mine”?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Genesis ended with Joseph’s death in Egypt and a promise: “God will surely attend to you.” Then came several hundred years in which the Creator said not a word, and Jacob’s family grew into a nation of slaves. Yet the Bible says something important about that silence: the Israelites’ cry “ascended to God,” and the Lord “remembered His covenant.” Silence on the Creator’s part did not mean He was absent.

The man chosen to lead a nation out of slavery had a life story made of two crossed-out halves. The first was forty years at Pharaoh’s court, ending in a killing and a flight; the second, forty years as a shepherd of someone else’s sheep at the far edge of the wilderness. The call found him at his daily work. God spoke from a thornbush, the most ordinary plant in the desert, which burned and was not consumed, and He waited for Moses to come closer. He introduced Himself: “I am the God of your father.” He told Moses to tell the elders of Israel that He had attended to them, using the very Hebrew word the dying Joseph had left his brothers in the promise that God would attend to them. God picked up the conversation exactly where it had been left off, as if not a single day had passed.

Then He said, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people… I have heard them crying out… I am aware of their sufferings. I have come down to rescue them.” He called slaves “My people,” many of whom no longer remembered His name. He didn’t wait for them to improve before owning them as His. To the command “I am sending you to Pharaoh,” Moses replied with the question everyone knows who has faced a task too big for them: “Who am I?” God did not correct his self-assessment with a single word. He answered, “I will surely be with you.” The success of this mission did not depend on who Moses was, but on the One who went with him. God introduced Himself as “I AM WHO I AM.” That is not a definition but a promise of presence. Moses kept resisting, all the way to “send someone else,” but God did not withdraw the call; He patiently answered His servant’s objections one by one. The history of salvation is full of people who explained to the Lord that they weren’t fit for the job, and He did not agree with a single one of them.

Genesis ended with a coffin in the wrong country and a promise spoken over it: “God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land.” Then the story pauses for several hundred years. The family grows into a nation, hospitality turns into slavery, and through all that time God says not a word. He last spoke to Jacob before the journey to Egypt. His next sentence will come from a burning bush. Today we begin the section “There Is Hope When There’s No Way Out,” and we begin it in the very middle of that silence. The Bible says something important about God’s silence: “The Israelites groaned and cried out under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God. So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant.” Silence on the Creator’s part was not His absence.

sections.heading: Forty Years After It All
paragraphs: The man God chose for this mission had a life story made of two crossed-out halves. For the first forty years he was a prince at Pharaoh’s court: educated, well placed, with access to power. Even then he wanted to set people free, only in his own way. One day he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looked around to make sure no one was watching, and took justice into his own hands. It ended with a dead Egyptian, Moses on the run, and forty years during which the slavery went on. For the next forty years he was a shepherd of someone else’s sheep at the far edge of the wilderness, a man who had married into his father-in-law’s family, with no property and no plans. If a church were drawing up a list of candidates for a great work, an eighty-year-old shepherd with a killing in his past and a failed career would not even make it into the discussion. That is exactly the man God started a conversation with. And He didn’t pull him out of his everyday life; He stepped into it. Moses “was shepherding the flock of his father-in-law Jethro,” doing exactly what he did every day, when he “came to Horeb, the mountain of God.” The call found him at work.

sections.heading: A Bush That Did Not Burn Up
paragraphs: “There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush. Moses saw the bush ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed.” Not a cedar, not an oak, not some majestic tree. A thornbush, the most ordinary plant in the desert, the kind a shepherd walks past by the hundreds, good for kindling at best. God chose a worthless thing for His revelation and did not let it burn up. It’s hard to imagine a better picture of what He is about to say about Israel: a people in the fire of slavery who will not be consumed, because God is in the middle of it. One sentence in this account is easy to miss: “When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called out to him.” First a curious human step, then the voice. The Lord waited for Moses to turn aside from his path. How many things have we never heard because we didn’t bother to go over and look?

sections.heading: Take Off Your Sandals
paragraphs: The first instruction has nothing to do with Egypt or the mission: “Do not come any closer… Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” That sentence turns the religious geography of the time upside down. Holy ground was where a temple stood, a statue, an altar, where priests performed their service. Here, though, a patch of desert beyond the pasture turns out to be holy ground, with no building and no worship, simply because God chose to stop there. Holiness doesn’t live in architecture. It follows presence. A shepherd takes off his sandals at his workplace, on an ordinary day, halfway through his rounds with the flock. Perhaps that is why so many people have missed God: they waited for Him in solemn places, and He stopped beside their everyday work.

sections.heading: The God of Your Father
paragraphs: The voice from the bush calls him by name, twice: “Moses, Moses!” God called like that only to people for whom He had special plans. Then He introduces Himself with a sentence that is the key to the whole scene: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Right after that we hear an echo of events long past. The dying Joseph left his brothers a promise: “God will surely attend to you.” At the bush the Lord tells Moses to tell the elders of Israel, “I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt,” and in Hebrew this is exactly the same word Joseph used before he died. God picks up the conversation where it was left off several hundred years earlier, as if not a day had passed. For Moses this meant something more. He grew up at a foreign court, among foreign gods, and his first bond with his own people was his mother, hired by Pharaoh’s daughter as his nurse. God tells him: I am the God of your father. Your story did not begin in the palace, and it did not end with your flight. It is longer than your mistakes.

sections.heading: I Have Indeed Seen
paragraphs: Then God speaks about what He has seen: “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt. I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors, and I am aware of their sufferings. I have come down to rescue them.” Four verbs: I have seen, I have heard, I am aware, I have come down. There is a pattern in Scripture: when God says He sees someone’s oppression, it means He intends to rescue them from it. His seeing is not mere watching; it is the start of a journey. And we already know the direction from Bethel: it isn’t man who climbs up to God; it is God who comes down. “I have come down” to the bush and the stairway let down from above over the sleeping Jacob are the same movement. Notice whom the Almighty calls “My people.” Not a prayerful, faithful community, but slaves, most of whom had not heard His voice for generations, and many of whom were steeped in the gods of Egypt. God didn’t wait for them to improve before owning them as His. He called them His people when they were at the lowest point of their lives, and only then did He begin to lead them. We like to reverse that order, in the church too: first let someone start living right, then they can be one of us. With God, “Mine” comes before “improved.”

sections.heading: Who Am I?
paragraphs: “Therefore, go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.” And here Moses asks the question familiar to anyone who has ever felt that a task was too big for them: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” Forty years earlier he would have answered differently. Back then he was self-assured, strong, ready to dispense justice with his own hands, and that was exactly when he wasn’t fit for the job. Now, when he thinks he isn’t ready, God calls him. Interestingly, a second question built the same way will soon be asked in this same book. Pharaoh will ask, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?” Two questions about identity: a man’s humble question about himself and a ruler’s proud question about God. The answer to both is what the rest of the book is about.

The most interesting thing, though, is God’s answer to Moses’ question. God doesn’t say: you’re exaggerating, you’re perfectly prepared, a royal education plus years in the wilderness make an ideal résumé. He doesn’t correct his self-assessment with a single word. He says, “I will surely be with you.” To the question “Who am I?” He answers, “I will be.” Because the success of this mission doesn’t depend on who Moses is, but on who goes with him. Isaac heard that same sentence, and Jacob at Bethel, and Joshua, Gideon, and Jeremiah will hear it too, each at a moment when the task is too big for them. God never treats a sense of inadequacy with compliments. He treats it with His presence.

sections.heading: I AM WHO I AM
paragraphs: Moses presses further: and when they ask me what Your name is, what should I tell them? “God said to Moses, ‘I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: “I AM has sent me to you.”’” This name is not a definition that can be learned or a formula that can be controlled. It is a promise of presence, stretching into the future: I will be there wherever you are. The gods of Egypt had statues, addresses, and office hours. This God introduces Himself by presence alone. The name also appears in the New Testament. Centuries later a certain Teacher from Nazareth will say in Jerusalem, “before Abraham was born, I am!”, and His listeners will pick up stones, because they understand perfectly what He is referring to. The name from the bush did not stay in the book of Exodus. It came to people in person.

God also gives Moses a very strange sign: “this will be the sign to you that I have sent you: When you have brought the people out of Egypt, all of you will worship God on this mountain.” The proof of God’s sending will come only after leaving Egypt, although before that Moses will also receive other signs. Faith doesn’t always get full confirmation in advance.

sections.heading: Send Someone Else
paragraphs: The conversation at the bush did not end with a confession of faith. Moses will raise more objections: that they won’t believe him, that he isn’t eloquent, that he is “slow of speech and tongue,” until at last he says outright what lay beneath all the excuses: “Please, Lord, send someone else.” God answered every objection in turn, gave signs, gave him Aaron as a helper, but one thing He never did, not once: He did not withdraw the call. He didn’t say: you’re right, I’ll look for someone more reliable. The history of salvation is full of people who tried to explain to God that they weren’t fit for the job, but the Lord agreed with none of them. It is also worth remembering what the Creator did not do with Moses’ excuses: He did not treat them as a disqualification. He answered each one. The patience of this conversation is as much a part of God’s self-revelation as His name.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This scene sets the way we look at the whole section we are beginning today. When there’s no way out in sight, hope doesn’t begin with the situation getting better, but with God saying: I have seen, I have heard, I am aware, I have come down. And then He usually does the least expected thing: He sends a person, often one who has just finished proving to himself that he isn’t fit for the job. Maybe you carry a crossed-out half of your life story inside you: wasted years, a burned-out calling, a decision after which everything was supposed to be smaller. The eighty-year-old shepherd at the bush is proof that God does not divide a life into the part that matters and the part that was wasted. And one more important thing for us as a community: God said “My people” about those who didn’t remember His name. The next time we decide someone is too far from the Lord for Him to be near them, let’s remember whom He claimed as His own at the bush.
